children.text: The largest and oldest public market in Cebu City, where thousands of vendors sell fruit, vegetables, seafood, dried fish, flowers, and handicrafts. A redevelopment that is building new market halls is in full swing and sections are shifting, but it is still the closest look you can get at everyday Cebu life, with haggling and street food at every turn.

Carbon Market is Cebu's largest public market, spread across downtown Cebu City between Colon Street and the port. Several market buildings, the lanes around them, and even the squares are lined with stalls, so it feels like one huge neighborhood, and locals simply call it "Carbon." Figures vary by source, but regular stallholders and ambulant vendors together are said to number about 6,000, and produce from across Cebu and the Visayas, as well as from Benguet in Luzon and from Mindanao, passes through here before spreading across the city.
The name comes from carbón, Spanish for coal. It is said that a coal depot used by the old Cebu Railway once stood nearby, and the sign at the market entrance reads "Est.
." The land belonged to the national government until a presidential proclamation handed it over to Cebu City in

, and over the years of fires and expansions, buildings such as Unit 1 (meat and seafood), Unit 2, and Unit 3 (fruit) appeared, along with a produce wholesale area known as the bagsakan. Old landmarks also remain in the middle of the market, such as Warwick Barracks, a former U.S. Army post, and Freedom Park, which commemorates independence.
Carbon is now in the middle of a major transformation. After Cebu City signed a 50-year joint venture with a Megawide subsidiary in
, Freedom Park was restored as a park (

), The Barracks food court opened on the old barracks site, and an interim market building went up where the fire-gutted Unit 2 once stood. Construction of the first of three new market buildings began in
December 2025
and was about 35% complete as of
August 2026
, with the aim of opening its lower market floors in
December 2026
. Vendors from the flower, native products, fish, and fruit sections are set to move first, so stall locations may differ depending on when you visit.

If you are expecting a tidy mall or a tourist market, you may be disappointed. Floors are wet, there are strong smells, and carts and motorbikes squeeze through the crowds. In return, you can taste tropical fruit at local prices and walk among colorful stalls and the sound of haggling, getting a vivid picture of an ordinary day for Cebu's working people. It suits travelers who love photography and street scenes and those who enjoy market food, and since the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross are a
10-minute
walk away, it fits easily into an old town itinerary.

Fruit that changes with the seasons, such as mangoes, bananas, papayas, rambutans, mangosteens, and durians, is piled high. At the fruit stalls around Unit 3 you can buy Cebu mangoes by the kilo, and it is fine to buy just one or two and ask the vendor to slice them on the spot. It is customary to ask the price first and agree on it.

blocks.title: See the early-morning vegetable wholesale market

children.text: At the wholesale area called the bagsakan and the surrounding streets, cabbages, carrots, and tomatoes brought overnight from mountain villages and other islands are unloaded. Porters and traders are busiest around sunrise, so early morning is best if you want to watch the market wake up.

In the wet market around Unit 1, fish, squid, shrimp, and shellfish that arrived that morning are laid out on ice. There are also shops selling dried fish and squid, so the smell is strong, but there is a lot to see. If you plan to buy dried seafood as gifts, ask whether it can be vacuum-sealed.

Shops selling flowers and candles to offer at church, bamboo and rattan baskets, woven palm-leaf pouches for puso, brooms, and other everyday crafts are clustered here. This is one of the first sections set to move into the new market building, so its location may change; ask vendors as you look for it.

A food court modeled on Singapore's hawker centers, built on the site of Warwick Barracks, a former U.S. Army post. Stalls selling Cebuano dishes such as lechon, barbecue, tuslob buwa, and halo-halo are gathered under one roof, and there are also handicraft shops selling shell necklaces, baskets, and souvenir ukuleles. It is generally open

After dark, tented stalls go up along M.C. Briones Street and other streets around the market, selling fruit, vegetables, clothing, and grilled skewers until late. The city is discussing an ordinance to turn the long-standing practice of overnight trading in vegetables brought down from the mountains into an official night market, so check the latest information for days and hours.

blocks.title: Take a break at Freedom Park

children.text: A small square on the north side of the market, formerly known as Plaza Washington. The area, once packed with stalls, was cleaned up and restored as a park with an obelisk, walkways, and shady trees. It is a good place to catch your breath after wandering through the busy market.

items.title: Morning half-day course
items.subtitle: Market browsing and the old town

children.text: Arrive at Carbon by taxi or Grab. Watch vegetables being unloaded at the bagsakan wholesale area and the surrounding streets.
Walk the seafood and dried fish lanes around Unit 1. Watch your step, as the floor is wet.
Pick mangoes and seasonal fruit at the fruit stalls around Unit 3 and haggle over prices.
Browse baskets and everyday crafts in the flowers and native products section.
Rest in the shade of Freedom Park and eat the fruit you bought.
Walk to the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross and explore the old town.
Visit Fort San Pedro and finish with lechon for lunch.
Look around the Basilica del Santo Niño area first, then walk toward Carbon.
Stroll the market streets at dusk. The stalls are just lighting up, making it a great time for photos.
Have dinner of lechon, barbecue, and tuslob buwa at The Barracks food court and browse the handicraft shops.
Buy fruit and snacks at the evening stalls on M.C. Briones Street.
Head out to a main road and call a taxi or Grab back to your hotel.
Avoid walking alone down dark lanes deep inside the market late at night, and stick to the busy stalls along main roads and the food court.

The lanes inside the market are blocked by carts and stalls, so cars have a hard time getting through. It is quicker to get off on M.C. Briones Street or the main road near City Hall and walk in.
Jeepneys with "Carbon" written on the windshield go right to the market. Options include route 04B via Lahug and Capitol and route 13B from Talamban, and a ride costs about
. To be sure, ask "Carbon ni?" (Going to Carbon?) before boarding.
Jeepneys are crowded and prone to pickpocketing, so keep your bag on your lap. Route numbers and fares may change.

From Fort San Pedro, it is about

Fast ferries from Bohol reach Cebu's Pier 1 in about

, and from the pier to Carbon is a

The market is open all year, but the best time for walking around is the
December–May
dry season. Within that,
December–February
brings relatively cool mornings and evenings, while in
March–May
midday temperatures often exceed
, making the market lanes feel like a steam room. Mangoes tend to be most plentiful, and cheaper, in the later part of the dry season.
During the
June–November
rainy season, showers are frequent, and heavy rain quickly floods the streets around the market and turns them muddy. As with Typhoon Tino in
November 2025

, the whole of Metro Cebu can flood, so postpone your market visit if a typhoon warning is issued. Within the day, early morning, when goods are just arriving, is the liveliest and least hot. Around the third Sunday of
January
each year, during the Sinulog Festival, downtown roads are closed and crowds pour in, so getting to the market also takes longer.

There is no need to stay right next to Carbon. The streets around the market are dark and quiet at night in many places, so it is not recommended for first-time visitors. Business hotels around Colon Street and Fuente Osmeña, close to the old town, cost about
a night, while hotels around IT Park or Ayala Center, with plenty of restaurants and malls, cost about
. From there, the market is
20–40 minutes
away by taxi. Another option is to stay at a resort on Mactan Island and come into the city for half a day.

At the market, have fruit sliced on the spot and stave off hunger with banana fritters sold on the street (banana cue), grilled skewers, and charcoal-roasted corn. If you want to sit down to eat, The Barracks food court is the easiest choice. You can try Cebu's signature dishes in one place: lechon (whole pig roasted over charcoal), tuslob buwa, a broth made with pig brain and liver into which you dip puso, and halo-halo topped with mango. Small eateries and stalls are also gathered at Puso Village on the edge of the market.
If you plan to buy plenty of dried seafood as gifts, Taboan Market, about
2km
to the southwest, is better known. It specializes in danggit (dried fish) and dried squid and is
5–10 minutes
from Carbon by taxi. The smell clings easily to clothes, so ask for vacuum packing.
Goods are freshest and the heat is most bearable from
. The market is open from early morning until night and some stalls trade overnight, but hours differ by section.
Most vendors accept cash only. They often struggle to break ₱1,000 bills, so bring plenty of ₱20, ₱50, and ₱100 notes.
Haggling is the norm. Treat marked prices as a guide, and if you buy several items, ask with a smile for a small discount. Avoid bargaining too hard.
The floor is wet and slippery, so closed-toe shoes are better than sandals. The fish and dried seafood sections smell strongly, so a handkerchief or mask helps.

With fruit, asking the price per kilo before choosing causes fewer misunderstandings than asking after it is weighed. For mangoes, ask the vendor to separate ones to eat today from ones to eat in a few days, and they will pick them for you.
When photographing people or stalls up close, ask permission with a gesture first. Most people will smile and agree.
Bringing a shopping bag or sturdy tote makes it easy to keep fruit and dried seafood separate and cuts down on plastic bags.
Section locations change often due to redevelopment. If you are looking for a particular section, the quickest way is to ask vendors briefly, such as "Flowers?" or "Fruits?"

Carbon Market, Colon Street, and the area around the Basilica del Santo Niño are where pickpocketing and snatch theft are most common in Cebu. Wear your bag in front with the zipper closed, do not walk with your phone in your hand, and do not keep your wallet in a back pocket. Be especially careful when a crowd suddenly forms or someone strikes up a conversation and bumps into you.
Construction of the new market buildings continues throughout
, and vendor relocation schedules may change. Do not enter areas behind construction barriers, and check on-site signs and Cebu City's latest notices for section locations and access.
Carts, motorbikes, and tricycles pass constantly along the narrow lanes. Do not stop in the middle of the road to take photos.
Carry only as much cash and as many valuables as you need, and leave expensive watches and jewelry at your hotel.
Raw seafood and pre-cut fruit spoil easily in the heat. If you have a sensitive stomach, stick to fruit sliced in front of you.
At night, stick to the lit stalls along main roads and the food court, and use Grab or a metered taxi to get back. It is best not to take a taxi that refuses to turn on the meter.
